blocks.text: What product managers do in Linear on a Mac

Most product managers use Linear for three jobs. They keep the plan in projects, shape the work into issues, and check progress on boards. Each job has a Mac shortcut or two that saves time. This page walks through them in the order you will use them.

Expect sprint and cycle language in the interface. Some PMs find it developer-heavy. You can still run a clean product workflow with a few habits. Most of those habits come down to naming, structure, and where you keep the detail.
Install the Linear desktop app on your Mac

Download the app from Linear's download page. Linear offers builds for macOS on Intel, macOS on Apple silicon, and Windows. Pick the build that matches your chip. Choose Apple menu > About This Mac to see which one you have.

The desktop app updates itself in the background. Linear's docs say you can turn off auto-update with a defaults write command in Terminal, followed by a relaunch. Leave updates on unless your IT team controls versions. Otherwise you may miss changes like the September shortcut update.

items: Open Apple menu > About This Mac and note whether you have Apple silicon or Intel.
Install the desktop app, then sign in to your workspace.
Open Settings > Initiatives if your team wants initiatives. The feature is enabled there.
Check your plan on the pricing page before you invite the team. Team initiatives need Business or Enterprise.
Open a team project view and confirm that the timeline view is available.

blocks.text: Projects, initiatives, and issues: how the levels fit

Start with the three levels. An issue is one piece of work, like a bug or a spec task. A project collects issues toward a goal and a target date. An initiative groups projects around a company objective. Keep the three levels separate in your head, and the rest of Linear gets easier.

rows: One piece of work, such as a bug or a spec task
Belongs to one project at a time
A set of issues with a status, a single lead, and a target date
Only the name and status are required
A curated set of projects around a company objective
Team initiatives need Business or Enterprise
blocks.caption: The three levels in Linear, based on Linear's project and initiative docs.

blocks.text: Create a project with the + button in a workspace or team project view. Only the name and status are required. Each project has one lead field, so name one owner. Put the outcome in the description, and keep the name short enough to scan in a list.

An issue can belong to only one project at a time. When work spans two areas, pick the project that owns delivery. Then write the other area into the issue description and tag the lead of the second project. That keeps the issue in one place and the context in both.
When an initiative beats a bigger project

Use an initiative when one goal needs several projects. Here is a worked example. Say your team wants faster checkout this quarter. You create an initiative called Faster checkout, then add three projects: payment methods, cart speed, and address entry. Each project keeps its own issues, lead, and milestones.

An initiative is a curated set, not a filter. Project views collect work by filter. An initiative holds only the projects you add to it. Team initiatives need Business or Enterprise, so confirm your plan before you promise one to the team.
Milestones, project updates, and timeline views

Milestones mark stages in a project lifecycle. On the timeline, they appear as diamonds. Name each milestone after an outcome, such as Beta open to design partners, instead of a date alone. A reader can tell whether it is done without asking you.

Project updates summarize progress since the last update. They sit beside the property history, including target date changes, member changes, and milestone changes. Post an update on the same day each week, so the history reads like a log. Ask Lazur to draft the update from your notes, then dictate the final changes.

Timeline views appear on team project views, inside an initiative, and on the workspace projects view. They show projects and milestones. Linear does not offer an issue-level timeline, according to one third-party review.

blocks.title: No issue-level timeline
blocks.text: If stakeholders want a Gantt chart for every ticket, set expectations early. Put dates on projects and milestones instead. Link the detailed plan from the project description so people can find it.
Board layout shortcuts that save time on a Mac

Board layout groups issues by Status by default. You can add swimlanes for more structure. Switch between board and list with ⌘B. The keys below handle most of the reordering work, so your hands stay on the keyboard during a review.

items: ⌘B switches between board and list layout.
⌥⇧↑ moves the selected issue to the top of its column.
⌥⇧↓ moves the selected issue to the bottom of its column.
⇧X selects multiple issues so you can work through a batch.
S moves the selected issue to a new column. It lands at the top.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. Before a planning meeting, open the team board in board layout. Use ⌥⇧↑ to move the bug that blocks the launch to the top of its column. Press S to move a finished spec into the next column. The top of each column reads first, so urgent work belongs there.

A common mistake is dragging every card with the mouse. Keyboard moves are quicker, and they keep the board tidy during a review. Drag only when you need to move a card across columns in a way the keys cannot reach.
Board limits to know before you rely on it

Board layout has limits. Triage and Inbox do not support it. Cards do not show descriptions, so the detail has to live in the issue. You can set board as the default for a single view, but not for the whole workspace. Plan for these limits before you train a team on the board.
Issue templates for feature requests and bug reports

Templates save you from writing the same issue twice. Create a workspace template under Workspace settings > Templates. Create a team template under Team settings > Templates. A workspace template works on any team, but it cannot preset team labels or statuses. Use a team template when those presets matter.

Create an issue from a template with ⌥C. You can also click Template next to the team name in the issue creation modal. Inside a sub-issue, only templates without sub-issues appear. Build your top-level templates first, then add the sub-issue versions.

Form templates ask a requester for structured input. They can use Text, Long text, Dropdown, Checkboxes, Date, and Instructions fields. You can also add property fields for customer, label group, priority, title, and due date. Any field can be required.

Here is a feature request form that works for many PM teams. Add a required Text field for the problem in one sentence. Add a Long text field for customer evidence. Add a Dropdown for impact. Add a Date field for when the team needs an answer, and include the priority property.

Form templates can only be the default for non-team members. That makes forms a good intake path for people outside the product team, such as support or sales. Keep team workflows on standard templates.
Template mistakes to avoid

items: Expecting a workspace template to set team labels or statuses. It cannot.
Making a form the default for team members. Form templates only default for non-team members.
Looking for a template inside a sub-issue that has sub-issues. Only templates without sub-issues show up.
Worrying about a template cap. The docs state no numeric limit. Keep the list short anyway, so people pick the right one.

blocks.text: Recent Linear changes that affect PMs on a Mac
Linear ships changes often. Several recent updates change how a PM works on a Mac. Check the changelog once a month, or ask Lazur to research it for you.

items: Sept 3, 2026: ⌘N now creates whatever fits the current view. The command menu also got fuzzy search. Check your view before you press ⌘N.
Sept 14, 2026: Loops for product management can trigger on initiatives, projects, and cycles. They can edit documents and post Slack updates.
Sept 24: project lead teams and team-level project labels and statuses arrived.
Oct 22: custom loop templates arrived.
Nov 5: ⌘-click switches to an open desktop tab.

blocks.text: Ask Lazur to explain a changelog entry before you change your habits. Lazur reads what is on screen and answers out loud. That helps when a shortcut does something you did not expect after an update.
Plans and limits that change your setup

Plan limits decide what your team can do. The Free plan has a 250-issue cap and 2 teams. Basic adds more teams, but it does not include releases. Business adds team initiatives. Check the table before you commit to a plan.

blocks.text: Pick a plan by team shape, not price alone. A solo PM can work in Free until the backlog passes 250 issues. A team that wants initiatives across projects needs Business. Check the pricing page for monthly billing terms, since the published rates are billed yearly.
Where Linear falls short for product work

Third-party reviews name several gaps. Siit lists no issue-level timeline or Gantt, no native release management, one project and one assignee per issue, underpowered reporting, and a weaker mobile app. Siit is competitor-adjacent, so read it as one view, not a verdict.

A July 2026 write-up paraphrases Reddit discussions. It says PMs and designers find the language and sprint focus developer-oriented. It also cites missing subtasks, weak dependency management, and no custom views. That article links no threads and gives no counts, so treat it as a hypothesis to test.
Workarounds for the gaps

items: Releases: create a project per release, and use team labels to group the issues in it.
Dependencies: write each blocker in the project description. Name the blocking project and the date it needs to clear.
Reporting: post a weekly project update. The history of updates becomes your status report.
Language: write issue titles in plain words. Use templates to keep the structure your stakeholders expect.

blocks.text: None of these fix the gaps fully. They make the gaps cheaper to live with. Pick the two that hurt your team most, and start there.
How Lazur helps while you work in Linear

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask about anything on your screen. Lazur answers out loud. It is not a plugin, add-in, or partner for Linear, and it does not operate Linear for you.

Two modes matter most in Linear. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. You stay in control of every change.

Dictation covers the writing side. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Use it for issue descriptions and project updates. Snippets store text you repeat, like a standard update header. The personal dictionary keeps product names and team terms spelled correctly.
Questions to ask Lazur inside Linear

items: Explain the difference between a project and an initiative here.
Where is the timeline view on this page?
Walk me through adding a milestone, one click at a time.
Draft a project update from these notes. I will edit it by voice.
Remind me Friday to check the milestone dates.

blocks.text: Speak in full questions. Lazur answers better when it knows the goal. Say the outcome you want, not only the button name.
Privacy and what leaves your Mac

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer. The providers do not store them. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on your Mac.

Linear issues often hold customer names and internal plans. Check your company policy before you ask Lazur about that content. When in doubt, ask about the interface and leave the customer data out of the question.
Common mistakes product managers make in Linear

items: Putting one issue in two projects. It can belong to one project at a time, so pick the owner.
Skipping the project lead. Each project has a single lead field, so an empty field leaves the outcome without an owner.
Treating the board as the whole plan. Cards hide descriptions, so the detail belongs in the issue.
Pressing ⌘N without checking the view. Since Sept 3, 2026, it creates whatever fits the current view.
Assuming Free will last. The Free plan caps you at 250 issues, so count before you invite the team.

blocks.text: Your first week with Linear on a Mac

Start small. Set up one team, one project, and one template. Run a single weekly update for that project. Add more only after the habit sticks. A large setup is hard to keep up, so grow it one piece at a time.

faq.question: Is there a native Linear app for Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Linear ships a desktop app for macOS on Apple silicon and Intel. It updates itself in the background. Download it from Linear's download page, and check the docs if your IT team needs to control updates.

faq.question: What is the difference between a project and an initiative in Linear?
faq.answer: A project holds issues toward one goal, with a single lead and a target date. An initiative groups several projects around a company objective. Team initiatives need Business or Enterprise.

faq.question: Does Linear have a Gantt chart for every issue?
faq.answer: Linear does not offer an issue-level timeline, according to a third-party review. Timeline views show projects and milestones on team project views, inside an initiative, and on the workspace projects view.

faq.question: How much does Linear cost for a product team?
faq.answer: Free costs $0 and allows 250 issues and 2 teams. Basic costs $10 per user per month billed yearly. Business costs $16 per user per month billed yearly. Enterprise is custom. Check Linear's pricing page before you buy.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons in Linear for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps. It points at things, answers out loud, and guides you one click at a time. It is not a plugin or add-in, and Lazur has no partnership with Linear.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold its shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Why won't Linear let me put an issue in two projects?
faq.answer: An issue can belong to only one project at a time. Pick the project that owns delivery. Write the other area in the description, and tag its lead so they see the work.

faq.question: Does the Lazur trial need a credit card?
faq.answer: No. The Pro trial needs no credit card, and it starts when you first open the app. See the pricing page for the current trial length and plan prices.
